14.1.b:
Loosening is the slow end of a hip that was once well fixed; first, what it means and why we watch for it.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is aseptic loosening of a THA?"
- "A **late, cumulative** failure of a well-fixed implant: wear, debris, osteolysis, then loosening."
- "It is the **third** commonest indication for hip revision; in knee series it leads **late** revisions."
- "Exclude **infection** first, then look for the cause."

### Definition and Significance
Loosening is not a surgical slip on day one; it builds up over years.

#### Definition
- The septic or aseptic question and the work-up → 11 Painful arthroplasty
- The aseptic form is **cumulative**: the long-term fate of a well-fixed implant
- It is the **third** commonest indication for hip revision, after dislocation and infection (Handbook; Campbell)
- In knee series it leads **late** revisions, while infection leads early ones

#### Acetabular Loosening and Surveillance
- **Acetabular** loosening is often **asymptomatic**, so only serial X-rays find it
[[FIG: Fig 14.1 · 14.1
- So follow up **yearly**, then every **3 years**, then every **3–5 years** (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- A loose cup without pain is not revised; it is followed with serial X-rays
- But **severe or progressive** bone loss → consider revision even without disabling pain (Campbell)

MEMORY HOOK — the cat burglar
- A loose cup is a cat burglar: no noise, no pain, so only the yearly film catches it moving.

14.2.b:
Now the why: three layers of cause, one biological engine, and four ways a stem lets go.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why do hips loosen?"
- "Causes come in three layers: **mechanical**, **biological**, **technical**."
- "Debris is eaten by **macrophages**; **RANKL** wakes the osteoclasts; bone melts."
- "Cemented stems fail in **Gruen's four modes**; cantilever ends in stem fracture."

### Causes of Loosening
Each loose hip is asked three questions: what hit it, what it sat in, and how it was put in.

#### Three Categories of Cause

| Cause | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Mechanical** | acute or repeated trauma · extreme ROM (range of motion) · prior dislocation · old fracture |
| **Biological** | unhealthy bed: irradiated, diseased, brittle · **cemented** stem on poor stock · wear-induced **osteolysis** |
| **Technical** | thin **cement mantle** · **varus** stem, lateralised tip · instability · poor fracture fixation |

#### Technical Factors
- A **varus** stem takes more bending stress
- Bending brings micromotion and debris, and debris brings osteolysis
- Cement mantle thickness and technique → 02 Fixation & cement
- A badly managed intra-operative fracture counts as **technical**, not mechanical
- Cement needs good bone stock, so a **cemented** stem on a poor bed fails biologically

#### Patient and Implant Factors
- Early small **subsidence** of a cementless stem may settle into stable fixation (Campbell)
- Late or progressive subsidence means failed fixation
- **Young, heavy, active** patients have more long-term loosening

#### Clinical Example: Composite-Beam Stem
- Case: a **composite-beam** cemented stem lost its cement at 16 years
- Cement was left only in zone 1, and the stem subsided
[[FIG: Fig 14.2 · 14.2
- A **Wagner** stem was proposed, but it had to be **long**, as the old stem was long
- Done: a long cemented stem with a **dual-mobility** cup (Prof Sherif Khaled)

### Wear-Debris Osteolysis
The commonest biological road to loosening starts with tiny particles from the bearing.

#### Definition
- What wear is, its modes and bearings → 01 Bearings, materials & wear
- **Osteolysis** is the host bone's response to that debris
- The chain: wear → particulate debris → osteolysis → loosening
[[FIG: Fig 14.40 · 14.2

#### Clinical Features
- It is **silent**: extensive on film before any pain
- It is time-dependent, mainly **cell-mediated** inflammation driven by debris
[[FIG: Fig 14.3 · 14.2

#### Sources of Particles
- **Polyethylene** is the commonest source
- Then cobalt, titanium and **cement**
- Both wear and corrosion produce particles

#### Cells and Mediators
- **Submicron** particles (<1 µm) are the most active (Miller)
- **Macrophages** eat them, then release interleukins (**IL-1**, **IL-6**) and prostaglandin E2
- These are bone-resorbing cytokines

#### The Osteolytic Cycle
- **RANKL** activates the osteoclast, so bone is resorbed
- Resorption allows micromotion, and micromotion makes more wear

#### Treatment Principles
- Bisphosphonates and denosumab hit the osteoclast
- But established lysis needs the debris source removed

MEMORY HOOK — the hungry cleaner
- The macrophage is a cleaner who chokes on dust finer than 1 µm, then shouts (IL-6, RANKL) until the osteoclasts tear the walls down.

### Effective Joint Space
Debris does not stay at the bearing, so lysis turns up far away.

#### Concept
- Debris raises **hydrostatic pressure** in the joint
- Joint fluid creeps into every interface it can reach: the **effective joint space**
- So lysis appears at the stem tip, behind the cup and in screw holes
[[FIG: Fig 14.4 · 14.2
- In the void, a **periprosthetic synovial-like membrane** forms

#### Routes of Spread
- It tracks along the **bone–cement** or **bone–prosthesis** interface
- A **circumferential** proximal coating seals the path

#### Radiographic Appearance
| Lucency | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Linear** | loosening |
| **Expansile, scalloped** | particle osteolysis |

### Gruen Classification of Stem Failure
A cemented stem loses its grip in one of four patterns, and each leaves its own picture.

#### Four Modes
- Gruen zones and how to number them → 06 Post-op radiograph

| Mode (cemented stem) | Where fixation is lost | Picture |
|---|---|---|
| **1A Pistoning** | stem sinks inside the cement | mantle stable |
| **1B Pistoning** | stem and cement sink in bone | commonest cemented |
| **2 Medial midstem pivot** | fixed mid-stem, loose above and below | lucency superomedial and inferolateral |
| **3 Calcar pivot** | fixed proximally, loose distally | **windshield wiper**: distal ballooning |
| **4 Bending cantilever** | fixed distally, loose proximally | **stem fracture** |

#### Stem Fracture
- A **stem fracture** is a sure sign of a loose cemented stem
[[FIG: Fig 14.5 · 14.2
- It comes from the cantilever mechanism: the free top bends over the fixed tip
- The neck or neck–stem junction bends, and the head drops until it breaks

#### Definite Radiographic Signs
- A broken stem, or a fractured cement mantle
- A stem–cement lucency, or a change in stem position
[[FIG: Fig 14.6 · 14.2
- The drawings show where lucency and cement fracture appear in each pattern
[[FIG: Fig 14.7–14.8 · 14.2
- Case: lateral **cement fracture** and lucency in all zones = definitely loose, even if painless
[[FIG: Fig 14.37 · 14.2

#### Subsidence
- **1–2 mm** in the first year is normal (Prof Sherif Khaled)
- **2–5 mm** is a concern
[[FIG: Fig 14.9 · 14.2
- Why: the hollow, air-filled distal **centralizer** lets the stem sink 1–2 mm to lock the taper
- More than **2 mm** is abnormal
- Measure from the greater-trochanter tip, or head–neck junction, to the stem tip
- Use identical serial films, or the number means nothing

#### Pivot and Windshield-Wiper Patterns
- A pivoting stem swings and erodes one side
- Medial midstem pivot: on weight bearing the proximal stem goes **medial**, the tip **lateral**
- So compare weight-bearing with non-weight-bearing films
- A **wiper** is fixed proximally and toggles distally
[[FIG: Fig 14.10 · 14.2
- A calcar pivot shows best on **stress** or weight-bearing views

#### Clinical Example: Subsided Cemented Construct
- The construct subsided, the stem pistoned, and the **cement fractured**
[[FIG: Fig 14.11 · 14.2
- The distal opacity is the cement plug
- A **pedestal** belongs to cementless stems only

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Wear → debris → macrophage → RANKL → lysis · pressure spreads it · 4 Gruen modes, cantilever breaks the stem**

The clinical work-up belongs to chapter 11; this section keeps only the pointers and the imaging that plans a revision.

### Clinical Diagnosis
- Start-up pain, bloods, lucency, Harris and Engh grades → 11 Painful arthroplasty
- Infection and its treatment → 12 Periprosthetic joint infection

### Preoperative Imaging
A defect seen only in theatre is a defect not planned for.

#### Plain Radiographs
- Take **AP, lateral and Judet** views (Prof Ahmed Hazem)
[[FIG: Fig 14.12 · 14.3
- **Judet** views show the **columns**
- In a deformed pelvis a true AP or lateral is hard, so take all views
- Reference lines (walls, sourcil, teardrop, ilio-pubic, ilio-ischial) → 05 Planning
[[FIG: Fig 14.42 · 14.3
- Bone missing over the templated cup marks a deficiency
[[FIG: Fig 14.41 · 14.3

#### Computed Tomography
- Add **CT**, axial and coronal, in every complex case
- **Axial** cuts show walls, columns and floor thickness, so how far to ream
[[FIG: Fig 14.13 · 14.3
- **Coronal** cuts show superior cover
- A loose cementless cup with a cavity: CT finds the defect and a broken **medial wall**
[[FIG: Fig 14.38 · 14.3
- A cup more than **50% uncovered** must be reconstructed (Prof Ahmed Hazem)
- **3D CT** gives the best picture of the defect

14.4.b:
Loosening eats bone, so before any revision we name what is left.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you classify bone loss at revision?"
- "**Paprosky** asks what host bone is left to hold the implant, so it drives treatment."
- "**AAOS** (D'Antonio) describes where bone is lost: segmental, cavitary, combined, discontinuity, arthrodesis."
- "Contained takes morselised graft; uncontained needs structural support."

### Comparison of Classification Systems
Both systems are used, but they answer different questions.

| | Paprosky | AAOS (D'Antonio) |
|---|---|---|
| Built on | anatomy: host bone left (rim, floor, columns · metaphysis, diaphysis) | location of the loss |
| Style | decision-making | descriptive |
| Used for | **surgical decisions** (most used) | describing the defect |

- AAOS stands for American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
- AAOS (D'Antonio) dates from **1989**, Paprosky from **1994** (Campbell)
- The acetabulum is a cave: two columns, two walls, a dome and a medial wall
[[FIG: Fig 14.33 · 14.4
- **Contained** (cavitary) defects take **morselised** graft
[[FIG: Fig 14.34 · 14.4
- **Uncontained** (segmental) defects need **structural** support

### Paprosky Acetabular Classification
Paprosky reads the acetabulum by how far the cup has climbed and what still holds.

#### Types

| Type | Findings (Campbell) |
|---|---|
| **1** | supportive rim, no lysis, no migration |
| **2** | distorted hemisphere, columns intact, migration **<2 cm** |
| **2A / 2B / 2C** | 2A superomedial · 2B superolateral, no dome · 2C medial only |
| **3A** | migration **>2 cm** "up and out" · **Köhler intact** · 30–60% of cup on graft · loss 10 to 2 o'clock |
| **3B** | migration >2 cm "up and in" · **Köhler broken** · >60% on graft · loss 9 to 5 o'clock · discontinuity |

- The course version: type 1 rim intact, type 2 superior involvement, type 3 migrated
- Discontinuity, or a fracture through both columns, makes it **3B** whatever the bone loss (Handbook)

#### Radiographic Criteria
- **Superior migration** of the hip centre
[[FIG: Fig 14.14 · 14.4
- **Ischial** lysis means the posterior column is involved
- **Teardrop** lysis means the medial wall is involved
- A breach of the **Köhler** line

### AAOS Acetabular Classification
AAOS ignores migration and simply names the shape of the hole.

#### Types

| Type | Defect |
|---|---|
| **I Segmental** | rim lost, so **uncontained** |
| **II Cavitary** | volume lost, rim kept, so **contained** |
| **III Combined** | segmental plus cavitary |
| **IV Pelvic discontinuity** | superior and inferior halves separated |
| **V Arthrodesis** | fused hip: excess bone, not deficiency |

- Types I and II are **peripheral** (anterior, superior, posterior) or **central** (floor)
[[FIG: Fig 14.15 · 14.4
- Type I segmental: a lost rim, or a central hole in the medial wall
[[FIG: Fig 14.35 · 14.4
- **Combined** defects are uncommon in primaries and commoner at revision

#### Arthrodesis (Type V)
- First find the **true acetabulum**, using the teardrop and obturator foramen
- Assess the abductors first
- Example: a fused hip converted to a THA
[[FIG: Fig 14.43 · 14.4

### Paprosky Femoral Classification
On the femur, Paprosky asks one thing: how much isthmus is left to grip.

| Type | Bone left (Campbell) |
|---|---|
| **1** | minimal metaphyseal loss, diaphysis intact |
| **2** | extensive metaphyseal loss, diaphysis intact |
| **3A** | metaphysis unsupportive · **>4 cm** intact diaphysis |
| **3B** | metaphysis unsupportive · **<4 cm** intact diaphysis |
| **4** | metaphysis and diaphysis lost, wide canal, isthmus unsupportive |

- The key variable is the length of intact **isthmus** for distal fixation
[[FIG: Fig 14.16 · 14.4
- **Modular tapered fluted titanium** stems suit 3A and 3B, because they grip a short diaphysis

MEMORY HOOK — 2 up, 4 down
- Paprosky counts in centimetres: **2 cm** of cup climb upstairs, **4 cm** of isthmus downstairs.

### AAOS Femoral Classification
The femoral AAOS list adds deformity and narrowing to the hole types.

#### Types

| Type | Defect |
|---|---|
| **1 / 2 / 3** | segmental (cortical loss) · cavitary (endosteal widening) · combined |
| **4 / 5** | malalignment (trauma, osteotomy, metabolic disease) · stenosis (closed canal) |
| **6** | discontinuity (fracture) |

- The drawings show each femoral type
[[FIG: Fig 14.17 · 14.4

#### Malalignment and Stenosis (Types 4 and 5)
- Types 4 and 5 block a straight stem in good bone
- So plan an **osteotomy** or a custom stem
- An **extended trochanteric osteotomy** (ETO) gives access and corrects proximal deformity
- ETO for cement or a well-fixed stem → 17 Other hip complications
- Its length: ≥10 cm from the trochanter tip, leaving 4–6 cm diaphyseal fit (Prof Mahmoud Abdel Karim)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Paprosky: 2 cm migration, Köhler line, 4 cm isthmus · AAOS: segmental, cavitary, combined, discontinuity, arthrodesis**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you reconstruct a deficient acetabulum?"
- "The cup needs **≥50% living host bone**; graft only fills space."
- "Contained: ream and a bigger cup, with graft. Uncontained: augment, allograft or cage."
- "Discontinuity: **stabilise first**, then the cup."

### Principles of Reconstruction
Every reconstruction aims at the same three things (Prof Ahmed Hazem).
[[FIG: Fig 14.18 · 14.5

#### Goals
- Restore the **hip centre**: a lower joint reaction force means less wear and loosening
- Get **host-bone contact**
- Set the cup in a good position

#### Role of Host Bone
- Graft only fills space, so a cup sitting on graft migrates
- So the cup must contact the **posterior column and rim**

MEMORY HOOK — the filling and the foundation
- Graft is the filling, host bone is the foundation: never build the house on the filling.

### Contained Defects
A contained hole keeps its rim, so a bigger cup and graft are enough.

#### Management by Paprosky Type

| Paprosky type | Management |
|---|---|
| **1** | ream, larger porous cup (**jumbo**) · graft optional |
| **2** (A, B, C) | larger porous cup · **graft mandatory** |
| **2A–2C** | particulate or small block graft at the defect · 2C also a wafer-cut femoral-head floor |

#### Small and Large Cavitary Defects
- A **small cavitary** defect can be ignored
- The cup goes ≈**1 mm** larger
[[FIG: Fig 14.19 · 14.5
- A **large cavitary** defect, such as protrusio, takes morselised graft of **3–5 mm**
- It is packed in by **impaction grafting**
[[FIG: Fig 14.20 · 14.5

#### Extensive Cavitary Defects
- Use a **flanged** cup, more screws, or a **Müller ring**
[[FIG: Fig 14.21 · 14.5
- These protect the graft until it incorporates
- The rule: **≥50%** of the porous surface on host bone (Prof Ahmed Hazem)

#### Jumbo Cup
- A **jumbo cup** is ≈**66–80 mm** (Surgery of the Hip)
- It gives more host contact
- But it may raise the centre, and it removes bone

### Uncontained Defects
A lost wall must be rebuilt before a cup can sit on it.

#### Reconstruction Options
- **Paprosky 3** needs structural allograft (a figure-7 distal femur), **augments** or a **cage**
- The figure-7 graft can also come from a femoral head or proximal tibia
- A **half or full cage** over the graft is fixed to the ilium and ischium
- A **cup-cage** is one unit: a cup with a built-in cage

#### Segments Requiring Reconstruction
- An **anterior or inferior** segment can be ignored if the bone is good
[[FIG: Fig 14.22 · 14.5
- A **superior or posterior** segment is the main support, so reconstruct it
- A **column** must be rebuilt; posterior or superior walls are "not forgiving"
[[FIG: Fig 14.39 · 14.5

#### Conversion to a Contained Defect
- Allograft with screws, or augments, turns an **uncontained** defect **contained**
[[FIG: Fig 14.23 · 14.5
- A structural femoral-head graft is fixed with lag screws
[[FIG: Fig 14.24 · 14.5
- In a **combined** defect, fix the segment first, then fill the cavity
[[FIG: Fig 14.25 · 14.5

PITFALL — must the cup be cemented over augments?
- The Handbook says always cemented; Campbell uses a porous-metal augment with a **cementless** cup
- Cement only joins the cup to the augment (Campbell)
- Say → "**cementless cup on augments; cemented cup inside a cage or on bulk allograft**"

### Pelvic Discontinuity
When the pelvis is split in two, no cup can last until the halves unite.

#### Recognition and Principle
- It is usually an **ununited post-traumatic** acetabular fracture
- The principle: unstable → stable, so **stabilise first**, then add the cup or ring
[[FIG: Fig 14.26 · 14.5
- After the columns are fixed, **re-assess** and treat it as segmental or cavitary
- Suspect it when the **obturator ring** is broken
- Or when the hemipelves look rotated on Judet views

#### Acute and Chronic Discontinuity
| Discontinuity | Fix (Miller) |
|---|---|
| **Acute** | posterior-column plate, then cup |
| **Chronic** nonunion | cup-cage, triflange, or distraction |

- The cage and cup-cage constructs, and acetabular distraction
[[FIG: Fig 14.27 · 14.5

#### Revision Equipment
- Have graft, meshes, rings, augments, and protrusio and jumbo cups ready
[[FIG: Fig 14.28 · 14.5

### Treatment Algorithm
The whole cup side fits on one slide, sorted by the shape of the hole.

- Cavitary: small → over-ream · large → fill and protect (Prof Ahmed Hazem)
[[FIG: Fig 14.36 · 14.5
- Segmental: column or posterior/superior wall → reconstruct · anterior wall → ignore
- Combined: segmental first, then cavitary · discontinuity: stabilise rigidly, then re-assess

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Small cavity ignore, big cavity impact · segment augment · discontinuity stabilise**

14.6.b:
The femur follows one rule: fix the stem where good bone still is.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you reconstruct a deficient femur?"
- "Metaphysis good: fix there; metaphysis gone: fix in the **diaphysis**."
- "An extensively coated stem needs **≥4 cm** of isthmus; tapered fluted holds with less."
- "Little bone left: **impaction grafting**, a composite, or **proximal femoral replacement**."

### Paprosky Types 1 to 3A
While the isthmus is long enough, a longer or bigger stem does the job.

#### Management by Type

| Type | Management |
|---|---|
| **1** | ream, then a larger stem, no graft |
| **2** | larger porous stem, proximally **or** extensively coated |
| **3A** | diaphyseal fixation: extensively coated (≥8 inches) or tapered fluted stem |

- When the metaphysis fails, fixation moves down to the diaphysis
- Three fixation levels: metaphyseal, metaphyseal–diaphyseal, diaphyseal

#### Choice of Distal Fixation Stem
- An extensively coated stem needs **≥4 cm** of intact diaphysis (Miller)
- Its price is thigh pain and stress shielding
- A tapered fluted stem holds with **<4 cm**
[[FIG: Fig 14.29 · 14.6

MEMORY HOOK — park on firm ground
- A revision stem parks only on firm ground: if the metaphysis is mud, drive down to the diaphysis.

#### Clinical Example: Revision at 80
- Options: a long **Wagner**, a long locked modular, or a long cemented stem
- A standard stem is enough only if it is long enough
- Stem length varies by size: size 1 is 13.3, size 6 is 17.9 (Prof Sherif Khaled)

#### Clinical Example: Treatment
- Done: long cemented stem, **tripolar** head, cemented cup
[[FIG: Fig 14.30 · 14.6
- A low-demand patient accepts it

### Paprosky Types 3B and 4
When the isthmus is short or gone, bone must be rebuilt or replaced.

#### Reconstruction Options

| Option | Construct | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **Impaction grafting** | packed morselised graft and a polished tapered cemented stem (**Exeter**) | restores stock · slower |
| **Allograft–prosthesis composite** | stem cemented into a proximal allograft | restores stock · graft failure |
| **Proximal femoral replacement** | modular endoprosthesis | early weight bearing · poor abductor attachment |

#### Comparison of Options
- Impaction grafting rebuilds endosteal bone stock
[[FIG: Fig 14.31 · 14.6
- After proximal femoral replacement, reoperation is mostly for **instability**
- The choice rests on **age and demand**

#### Associated Periprosthetic Fracture
- Vancouver B3, long stems and the fracture decision → 15 Periprosthetic fractures
[[FIG: Fig 14.32 · 14.6
- Fracture with bone loss after poor cementing → 15 Periprosthetic fractures

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Femur: metaphysis, then diaphysis 4 cm · then impaction, composite or replacement**
